text:
—This is a guest post by Stephen Winik, a folklorist in the American Folklife Center. It also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

The American Folklife Center turns 50 in 2026, marking a half century of preserving, presenting and supporting folk culture. The celebration culminates in mid-September with the opening of a major exhibition, “Alive in Many Hands: The American Folklife Center at 50.”

The center owes its existence to the American Folklife Preservation Act of 1976. Congress charged it with safeguarding the nation’s living cultural traditions — everything from fiddle tunes and quilt patterns to holiday rituals, occupational skills and family recipes. These expressions belong to families, ethnic communities, work groups, religious congregations and regions, stretching from the mainland to the Caribbean and Pacific Islands.

Today, the center maintains one of the largest folklife archives anywhere. It exchanges knowledge and expertise with scholars and communities and produces public programs that bring these traditions to life.

“Alive in Many Hands,” part of the Library’s America 250 celebrations, pulls from the best of those collections to show how tradition thrives in countless hands across the country. The exhibit runs through early 2028.

Step into the exhibition, and the collections begin speaking.

A “crossing the line” certificate marks a rowdy rite of passage for World War II sailors crossing the equator for the first time. They were forced to perform silly tasks, subjected to teasing and trials and finally presented to King Neptune and his court — other sailors in disguise. Survivors earned the title “shellback” and a certificate to prove it.

A brick fragment from Luboml, whose Jewish inhabitants were executed en masse by the Nazis during World War II. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

Nearby in the exhibit, recorded sea shanties recall an earlier age of shipboard life, when songs kept crews working in rhythm aboard sailing vessels — massive machines of wood, canvas and rope.

A few feet away sits a small wooden puzzle from Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains. Raymond Nichols carved its pieces with a pocketknife so that, when assembled, they nest into a perfect ball. When Nichols gave it to AFC fieldworkers in 1978, he couldn’t remember when or where he learned to cut and shape the pieces into precise dimensions. “Must have seen it somewhere when I was a boy,” he said.

A skilled woodworker, Nichols built much of his own house and furniture, including a barn raised in the traditional Blue Ridge style used by generations of farmers. A modern building inspector wasn’t impressed, though — he rejected the poplar beams and the fieldstone foundation. Nichols chuckled as he recounted the story to AFC fieldworkers: “Boys, I’ll tell you — the pioneers wouldn’t stand a chance!”

Other objects carry a heavier weight, tell stories of vanished communities.

Documentarian Candacy Taylor (left) with New Orleans chef Leah Chase, whose restaurant appeared in the Green Book . Photo: Courtesy of Candacy Taylor.

A weathered directional sign and a single brick fragment come from Luboml, a once-thriving Jewish shtetl then in Poland, now part of Ukraine.

The sign stood on a corner just outside the Jewish Ghetto — a witness to the community’s destruction. On Oct. 1, 1942, Nazis marched residents of the ghetto to that very corner, then directed them on to a place where they would be executed en masse.

AFC holds dozens of oral histories of Americans who once called Luboml home, along with thousands of pages of manuscripts and photos. Together, they preserve the memory of a Jewish community erased by the Holocaust — as does that street sign, the only one of the Nazi era known to still exist.

“Alive in Many Hands” also traces stories of struggle and progress in the United States.

Published between 1936 and 1967, The Negro Motorist Green Book guided Black travelers to safe places to eat, sleep, shop and get gas — a vital resource during the segregation era.

Through oral histories collected by documentarian Candacy Taylor and held by AFC, exhibition goers meet some of the business owners like New Orleans chefs Dooky and Leah Chase who made the book — and safe travel — possible. When segregation ended, the Green Book disappeared, but its legacy of service to the Black community remains.

A dedicated section of the exhibit explores foodways — the rich cultures and traditions surrounding food.

No matter where we live, how we work or how we spend our time, food is a constant in all our lives. We have favorite (and not-so-favorite) dishes, traditional methods of cooking and deeply ingrained customs for obtaining, preparing, eating and sharing meals.

A World War II chocolate ration. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

The World War II chocolate rations, community cookbooks, military menus and mouthwatering photos of food and food preparation in the exhibit explore how food embodies our cultural traditions, shared experiences and our connections to the places we live, work and play.

Many other foodways items from the exhibit — along with compelling stories, photos and even songs about food and drink — will be featured in the forthcoming book “Sharing Food, Sharing Culture.” Part of the Library’s “Collections Close-up” series, the book is scheduled for publication in September.

Music runs through the exhibit like a living current.

Two photographs capture artists from AFC’s Homegrown concert series: Louisiana Creole accordionist Sean Ardoin and the Navajo duo Sihasin, artists who represent a long family history of music. Sean traces his lineage to legendary accordionist Amédé Ardoin, and Sihasin to community leaders, singers and dancers, including their father, Jones Benally. In their concert videos, online at loc.gov , they tell those family stories.

The photos also tell the tale of the concert series itself.

Folklorist Alan Lomax used a disc cutter like this one to record spirituals by Becky Elzy (left) and Alberta Bradford, two singers who grew up in slavery . Courtesy of E.A. McIlhenny Collection, Avery Island Archives, Avery Island, Louisiana.

Concerts have always been a part of American Folklife Center programming — the first event hosted by AFC, in February 1976, featured traditional folk music from prominent artists. When COVID shut down most social life in March 2020, AFC quickly adapted, hiring musicians to record performances wherever they could.

Sihasin, a brother and sister duo of Clayson and Jeneda Benally, performed on a windswept Arizona plain, joined by their father and their beloved horse, Moonwalker. Ardoin created a video of himself playing live with prerecorded tracks he had laid down himself. The results were powerful and intimate — and are still available on the Library’s website and the Folklife Today blog.

Technology itself gets a spotlight via a hefty Presto instantaneous disc recorder used by the Library in the 1930s and ’40s — one of a succession of technologies, from wax cylinders to reel-to-reel tapes, used to record traditional songs and stories.

The disc recorder was probably the heaviest of these technologies — and it required additional bulky equipment for playback and car batteries for power. Sometimes, the bulk and weight of these machines became part of the story.In June 1934, renowned folklorist John A. Lomax and his 19-year-old son, Alan, hauled one of these machines to Avery Island, Louisiana. The goal: record spirituals for the Library performed by Becky Elzy and Alberta Bradford — two elderly women who were born into slavery and lived through the Civil War and emancipation.

Elzy and Bradford always sang together, which presented a problem for the Lomaxes: They arrived to find that Elzy had moved 50 miles away to Lake Arthur. Drenching rains compounded the problem: The roads were deep mud, and the Lomaxes weren’t sure they could drive themselves, Bradford and the heavy equipment to Elzy without getting hopelessly stuck.

So, the elder (and heavier) Lomax stayed behind while Alan, Bradford and the equipment drove off to find Elzy. Reunited, Elzy and Bradford sang 10 spirituals, including a jubilant “Free at Last,” while Alan recorded — probably the first recordings the soon-to-be famous folklorist made without his father.

It’s awe-inspiring for anyone to hear “Thank God Almighty, I’m free at last” sung by women who suffered under slavery.

But two people were especially delighted when AFC published the recordings on the Folklife Today blog in 2019: Elzy’s great-great-granddaughter and Bradford’s great-great-grandson — neither of whom knew the recordings existed.

It’s through telling stories like this, connecting Americans to cherished aspects of our culture, that the American Folklife Center meets its mission. These are the stories you’ll find throughout “Alive in Many Hands.”

Subscribe to the blog— it’s free!
